title: A house open wide (Avot 1:5)
hookLine: let your house be open wide, and let the poor be members of your household

lines: THE HOUSE YOU JUST WALK INTO.
cards: Some homes you just walk into. The door's unlocked, there's always something on the stove, and nobody asks why you came. Kids from down the street end up at dinner.
A cousin sleeps on the couch for a month. Other homes, lovely ones, are closed: you visit by appointment, and you leave before it gets awkward. Plenty are somewhere in between.
The first Yose opened his house to the wise. His partner, Yose from Jerusalem, goes further. Not just the wise.

teach.b: Yose ben Yochanan of Jerusalem says, in paraphrase: let your house be open wide, and let the poor be members of your household. In Hebrew, open wide is patuach lirvacha.
Revach means space, room, relief: a house where someone in trouble can breathe.
The rabbis pictured Abraham's tent. A midrash says it had openings on all four sides, so a traveler coming from any direction would find a door facing them.
In Genesis, Abraham runs out in the heat of the day to greet three strangers. That's the model.
Then the second half: let the poor be members of your household. Not guests at the back door. Not a donation in an envelope.
Family. At the table, in the conversation, known by name. Some commentators note the dignity in it: a poor person treated like a member of the house doesn't have to feel ashamed to be there.

The same saying continues with a warning against too much idle talk with women, words that some readers today find troubling, and that commentators over the centuries have explained, limited and argued about.
I won't pretend it isn't there.
But the first line is the one to carry today: an extra chair at Shabbat dinner, a stranger at the seder, a door that opens easily.

how: Hachnasat orchim, welcoming guests, is a Jewish practice: guests are invited to Shabbat and holiday meals, and early in the seder the Haggadah invites all who are hungry to come and eat.

o: open-handed, giving freely to charity outside
open wide, a home with room for anyone in need
an open book, a life with nothing kept hidden

games.q: the open house — tap the pairs.

s: Yose ben Yochanan says to give to the poor at the door
he says to let the poor be members of your household, part of the family.
a midrash says Abraham's tent had openings on all four sides
so travelers from any direction would find a way in.
the whole saying is easy for modern readers
its second half warns against idle talk with women, which some readers find troubling and commentators have debated.

games.q: you're hosting Shabbat dinner. there's a neighbor who lives alone and has nowhere to go. what does Yose ben Yochanan say?
o: drop off a plate at their door.
bring them to the table as part of the household.
games.why: let your house be open wide, and let the poor be members of your household: at the table, not at the door.

practice: Picture your front door, and who hasn't come through it in a long time, or ever: a neighbor who lives alone, a new coworker far from home, someone in a hard stretch, a student with nowhere to go on a holiday.
Picture them at your table. Then choose one simple invitation you could offer: coffee, a walk, a plate of leftovers.

wordCard.voice: Patuach lirvacha. Open to spaciousness: Yose ben Yochanan's saying that a house should open wide, with the poor as members of the household.

orig.note: Hebrew: open wide, open to spaciousness (Avot 1:5).

carryVoice: Your line: open the door wide. Wide enough that anyone, from any direction, finds a way in. See you tomorrow.
